passages.happening:
Jesus has been praying. When he finishes, one of his disciples asks, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples” (verse 1).

Jesus gives them a prayer: “Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation” (verses 2-4).
passages.hearers:
Matthew gives this prayer in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:9-13), and the note there explains its words. ‘Hallowed’ means treated as holy. The word for ‘daily’ is rare and hard to pin down; the prayer asks for enough, one day at a time. ‘Temptation’ can also mean ‘test’ or ‘trial’.

Luke's form is shorter. It begins with the single word ‘Father’, not ‘Our Father in heaven’. It has no ‘Your will be done’ and no ‘deliver us from the evil one’. Where Matthew says ‘debts’, Luke says ‘sins’. If your Bible has a longer version here, as the King James Version does, it is because many later copies of Luke filled in lines from Matthew. The oldest copies have the shorter form. Some think Jesus taught the prayer more than once, in different words; others think the two Gospels kept it as different churches prayed it. Either way, both forms are the Lord's Prayer.

The setting is Luke's own. Jesus is praying, and the disciples want what they see. John the Baptist had taught his followers to pray. The disciples are asking for a prayer of their own, as Jesus' people.
passages.ot: Israel already knew God as Father: “You, O LORD, are our Father” (Isaiah 63:16). In the wilderness God gave manna every morning, “enough for that day” (Exodus 16:4). And a wise man prays, “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion” (Proverbs 30:8).
passages.hard:
‘Forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us.’ Does that mean God's forgiveness depends on ours? Most Christian traditions say no. The note on Matthew 6:9-15 explains that forgiving others is the sign that God's forgiveness has really reached us, not the price of it.

Forgiveness has also been misused. Some have told people who were abused to forgive quickly, keep quiet, or go back to the person who hurt them. That is not what this prayer asks. Forgiveness lets go of revenge. It is not the same as trusting someone again, and it does not mean a crime should go unreported. A person can forgive and still stay safe, still tell the truth, and still ask for justice. It can also take a long time, and that is not failure.
passages.asks: The disciples did not ask, ‘Teach us about prayer.’ They asked, ‘Teach us to pray.’ Try the prayer slowly, in Luke's short form, one line at a time. Notice that it begins with ‘Father’ and that its first wish is for God's name and kingdom, before any of our needs. Where do you stop when you pray it?

passages.t: A friend at midnight; ask, seek, knock
passages.happening:
Jesus tells a short story. Suppose you go to a friend at midnight and say, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread. A friend of mine has arrived after travelling, and I have nothing to give him.’ And suppose your friend calls from inside, ‘Do not bother me. The door is shut, and my children and I are in bed.’ Jesus says, “even though he will not get up to provide for him because of his friendship, yet because of the man’s persistence, he will get up and give him as much as he needs” (verse 8).

So, “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you” (verse 9). What father, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake? Or a scorpion for an egg? “So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke has the friend at midnight. Hearers would feel its force at once. Welcoming a guest was a serious duty, and to have nothing to set before him was a shame for the host. The sleeper's own words show the other side: the door is shut for the night, and his children are in bed with him.

The key word in verse 8 is hard to translate. The BSB says ‘persistence’. The Greek word, anaideia, is found only here in the New Testament. Its usual meaning in Greek is ‘shamelessness’, a lack of proper shame. So readers take the story in two main ways. Many, following older Bibles, think it means the man at the door kept on knocking until he was given what he asked: so keep praying. Others think the word means the asker's boldness in waking a friend at midnight, or that it belongs to the sleeper, who gets up to avoid the shame of refusing a neighbour. Scholars still argue about it. On every reading the story makes the same final point, and Jesus spells it out: if even a sleepy neighbour will get up, how much more will God, who is not sleepy and not reluctant.

Matthew has ‘ask, seek, knock’ too (Matthew 7:7-11), and the note there explains it. Luke adds the egg and the scorpion, and he changes the ending. In Matthew the Father gives ‘good things’. In Luke he gives the Holy Spirit.
passages.ot: The Old Testament knows a God who hears: “The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth” (Psalm 145:18). Through Jeremiah God says, “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13).
passages.hard:
Does Jesus promise that we will get whatever we ask for? A skeptic can fairly point to prayers that were not answered. Some teachers have claimed that faith always brings health and money, and have blamed people when it did not. That is not what this passage teaches.

Luke's ending shows what the promise is about. The gift Jesus names is the Holy Spirit: God's own presence. A good father does not give a child everything the child asks for, and he never gives a snake when asked for a fish. In the garden Jesus himself prayed for the cup to pass, and then said, “yet not My will, but Yours be done” (22:42). So most Christians read these words as a call to keep praying, to a Father who listens and gives what is good, not as a key to make God do what we want. The question of unanswered prayer is real, and this passage answers it with trust in a Father, not with a formula.
passages.asks: The man at the door had nothing for his guest, and he went to the one who had bread. Ask what you have run out of: patience, hope, love for someone. And notice what Jesus says the Father most wants to give: not just bread, but the Holy Spirit himself. Is that something you have asked for?

passages.happening:
Jesus drives out a demon that has made a man mute, and the man speaks. The crowds are amazed. But some say, “It is by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons, that He drives out demons” (verse 15). Others want a sign from heaven.

Jesus knows what they are thinking. A kingdom divided against itself is ruined. If Satan is divided against himself, how can his kingdom stand? And if Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do their own sons drive them out? “But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (verse 20).

A strong man, fully armed, guards his house. But when someone stronger overpowers him, he takes away his armour and divides the plunder. “He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this argument too (Mark 3:22-30; Matthew 12:22-30), and their notes explain it. Beelzebul goes back to Baal-zebub, “the god of Ekron” (2 Kings 1:2), and by Jesus' day it had become a name for the chief of evil spirits. Other Jews also drove out demons in those days, which is why Jesus asks about ‘your sons’.

Luke's picture of the strong man is fuller. The strong man is ‘fully armed’, and the stronger one ‘takes away the armor in which the man trusted’. It sounds like a battle and a victory.

Where Matthew says ‘the Spirit of God’, Luke says ‘the finger of God’. Both mean God's own power. Luke keeps the warning about the sin against the Spirit for later (12:10).
passages.ot:
‘The finger of God’ comes from the Exodus. When Moses' signs in Egypt went beyond what Pharaoh's magicians could copy, they said, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19). The tablets of the Law were “inscribed by the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18). Jesus' hearers would catch it: God is at work as he was when he set Israel free.

The strong man comes from Isaiah: “Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved” (Isaiah 49:25).
passages.hard:
‘He who is not with Me is against Me’ sounds like the opposite of 9:50, ‘whoever is not against you is for you’. The note on Luke 9:46-50 explains that they answer different questions. There, someone is doing good in Jesus' name outside the disciples' group: let him be. Here, the question is Jesus himself, and no one can stay neutral toward him.

A word on illness. Luke tells this man's silence as the work of a demon. But Luke also keeps sickness and possession apart as different needs (6:18; 7:21). As the note on Matthew 9:32-34 says, the Gospel does not teach that every disability or illness has an evil spirit behind it, and it would be wrong and cruel to say so of anyone today.
passages.asks: Some in the crowd saw a man who could speak again and called it evil, because they had already decided about Jesus. Ask whether you have refused to call something good because of who did it. And hear the last line: there is no neutral ground. Are you gathering with him, or only watching?

passages.t: The empty house, and who is blessed
passages.happening:
When an unclean spirit leaves a man, it wanders through dry places looking for rest. Finding none, it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’ It finds the house swept clean and put in order. So it brings seven other spirits worse than itself, and they live there. “And the final plight of that man is worse than the first” (verse 26).

As Jesus is saying this, a woman in the crowd calls out, “Blessed is the womb that bore You, and blessed are the breasts that nursed You!” (verse 27). He answers, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Matthew has the empty house too (Matthew 12:43-45), and the note there explains it. In Luke it comes right after the strong man. Being set free is not enough. A swept house with no one living in it is an open door.

Only Luke has the woman in the crowd. Her cry was a natural way to praise a man: blessed is his mother. It also honours Mary, and Luke has already called her blessed (1:42, 48). Jesus does not deny it. But he turns the blessing outward, to anyone who hears God's word and keeps it. Mary herself is the first example. When the angel came, she said, “May it happen to me according to your word” (1:38).
passages.ot: The Old Testament pictures the desert and ruined places as the home of wild and lonely creatures, the opposite of a living city (Isaiah 34:14). And it blesses the hearer who obeys: “Blessed is the man who listens to me” (Proverbs 8:34).
passages.hard:
Does this passage teach that illness, especially mental illness, is a spirit that can return? No. As the note on Matthew 12:43-45 says, Jesus is telling a parable, and it is not a medical teaching. It does not mean that someone whose illness comes back has let in a demon. Illness of body or mind is illness. If something you have struggled with has returned, that is not a judgment on your faith. Please get help again: a doctor, a pastor, or a crisis line.

Is verse 28 a put-down of Mary? Christians have read it differently. Some hear Jesus correcting too much honour to his mother. Many others, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant alike, note that Luke shows Mary as the one who heard the word and kept it (1:38, 2:19). On that reading Jesus is not lowering his mother but showing what made her blessed, and opening the same blessing to everyone.
passages.asks: A clean, empty house is not safe. Ask what fills the space where an old sin or habit used to be. And ask whether you are content to admire Jesus from the crowd, or whether you are hearing his word and doing it.

passages.t: The sign of Jonah, and the lamp of the body
passages.happening:
As the crowds grow, Jesus says, “This is a wicked generation. It demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah” (verse 29). As Jonah was a sign to the people of Nineveh, so the Son of Man will be to this generation. The Queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and the men of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching. Both will stand up at the judgment against this generation. “Now One greater than Solomon is here” (verse 31), and one greater than Jonah.

Then he speaks of light. No one lights a lamp and hides it. “Your eye is the lamp of your body” (verse 34). When your eye is good, your whole body is full of light; when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. “Be careful, then, that the light within you is not darkness” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Matthew tells this too (Matthew 12:38-42), and the note there explains it. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had crushed the northern kingdom of Israel; it was the last city a Jew would expect to repent. The Queen of the South is the queen of Sheba. Two outsiders, an enemy city and a foreign queen, responded to less than what was now in front of Jesus' hearers.

Luke's sign of Jonah is simpler than Matthew's. Matthew compares Jonah's three days in the fish to Jesus' three days in the grave. Luke says only that Jonah himself was a sign to Nineveh, a man who came to them with God's message. Jesus is that sign now, standing in front of them.

‘Wicked generation’ is spoken as the prophets spoke, to their own people. Christians have sometimes turned words like these against the Jewish people as a whole. That is a misuse. The warning is for every generation that sees God at work and still demands more proof, including our own.

Matthew has the lamp of the body in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:22-23), and the note there explains it. In Hebrew speech a ‘good eye’ could mean a generous one and a ‘bad eye’ a grudging one. The eye is like a window: what it lets in fills the whole person.
passages.ot: Jonah preached, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” and “the Ninevites believed God” (Jonah 3:4-5). The queen of Sheba “came to test him with difficult questions” (1 Kings 10:1). A psalm says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105).
passages.hard: Why will no sign be given, when Jesus did so many signs? The crowd had just seen a mute man speak (11:14). What they wanted was proof on their own terms, something from heaven that would force belief. Jesus refuses that. The sign he gives is himself, his word and, in the end, his rising from the dead. Faith that waits for overwhelming proof before it will move is not what God asks.
passages.asks: A pagan city repented at the preaching of one reluctant prophet. A queen travelled far on a rumour. Ask what you have been waiting for before you take Jesus seriously. And check your eyes: what are you letting in, and is it filling you with light or with darkness?

passages.happening:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to a meal, and Jesus reclines at the table. The Pharisee is surprised that Jesus does not wash first.

Jesus says, “you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness” (verse 39). Did not the one who made the outside make the inside too? “But give as alms the things that are within you, and you will see that everything is clean for you” (verse 41).

Then three woes. “Woe to you Pharisees! You pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but you disregard justice and the love of God” (verse 42). They should have done the one without neglecting the other. Woe to them, for they love the best seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. “Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, which men walk over without even noticing” (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Matthew gathers woes like these into one long speech in the temple (Matthew 23), and the note there explains them. Luke sets them at a dinner table, as a conversation with a host. Jesus keeps accepting Pharisees' invitations in Luke (7:36; 11:37; 14:1). He argues with them because they are close to him, not far away.

Who were the Pharisees? Here it matters to get them right. They were a movement of devout Jews, most of them not priests but lay people, who tried to keep God's law in the whole of ordinary life, at home and at work, not only in the temple. Some of them warned Jesus that Herod wanted to kill him (13:31). So ‘Pharisee’ is not a word for a hypocrite. In later Christian speech it came to mean that, but it did not mean that to Jesus' hearers.

The washing was not about dirt. It was a ritual washing of the hands before a meal. The Greek word is the one that gives us ‘baptize’. Priests washed before they served at the altar, and many Pharisees tried to bring that kind of holiness to the ordinary family table. The note on Mark 7 explains the custom.

A tithe was a tenth given to God. Some careful people tithed even their kitchen herbs. Luke names rue, where Matthew names dill and cumin. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, lists rue among plants that did not need to be tithed at all (Mishnah Sheviit 9:1). If that rule was known in Jesus' day, these men were going beyond what the law asked. Jesus does not mock it. He says they should have done it, without neglecting justice and the love of God.

Luke's grave picture is the opposite of Matthew's. In Matthew, the tombs are whitewashed: bright outside, death inside. In Luke, the graves are unmarked. Touching a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16), and people walk over these without knowing. Jesus means that people who follow these teachers are being made unclean without realising it.
passages.ot:
Jesus' ‘justice and the love of God’ echoes the prophets. “And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). God says through Hosea, “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

The woe itself is an old prophetic cry, used by Jews speaking to their own people. Isaiah cried, “Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land” (Isaiah 5:8).
passages.hard:
Has this chapter been used against Jewish people? Yes, for centuries. Christians read the woes as a verdict on the whole Jewish people and used them to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is wrong, and this site rejects it plainly. The woes are a warning to religious leaders, never a verdict on the Jewish people. They are spoken by a Jew, at a Jewish host's table, in the voice of Israel's own prophets.

And the woes fall first on religious leaders of every age, Christian ones included. Loving the best seats, keeping small rules while neglecting justice, cleaning the outside and leaving the inside full of greed: every one of these has fitted Christian pastors, priests and teachers. The New Testament says that “we who teach will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1). These words are rightly read when a Christian reader finds himself in them first.

And was Jesus rude to his host? By the standards of a polite dinner, perhaps. But the prophets were never polite about justice. Jesus spoke hard words to people he cared enough to eat with.
passages.asks: Jesus said, ‘Give as alms the things that are within you.’ A clean heart shows itself in open hands. Ask what you are careful about in your faith, and whether you are as careful about justice and the love of God. And ask whether anyone has been harmed by following your example without knowing it.

passages.t: Woes on the experts in the law
passages.happening:
One of the experts in the law says, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well” (verse 45).

Jesus answers with three more woes. They load people with heavy burdens and will not lift a finger to help. They build tombs for the prophets their fathers killed. So the blood of all the prophets, “from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary” (verse 51), will be charged to this generation. “Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key to knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering” (verse 52).

When Jesus leaves, the scribes and Pharisees begin to oppose him fiercely, firing questions at him and waiting to catch him in something he might say.
passages.hearers:
The experts in the law were the scholars who explained the Law of Moses: the same kind of man who asked about eternal life in 10:25. The note on Matthew 23 explains these woes in Matthew's longer form.

The ‘heavy burdens’ were the many detailed rules built up around the Law. The charge is not that rules are bad, but that the teachers laid them on others without helping anyone carry them.

Abel was the first person murdered in the Bible (Genesis 4). The Zechariah killed ‘between the altar and the sanctuary’ is most likely the priest stoned in the temple court in the days of King Joash (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). In the usual order of the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles comes last, though scholars debate whether that order was already fixed in Jesus' day. So ‘from Abel to Zechariah’ means from the first murder in Scripture to the last.

‘The key to knowledge’ is the key to understanding Scripture, which should open the way to God. These teachers held it, and used it to lock the door.
passages.ot:
When Cain killed Abel, God said, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Zechariah's last words were, “May the LORD see this and call you to account” (2 Chronicles 24:22).

The prophets warned teachers who misled. “For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge”, Malachi says, but “your instruction has caused many to stumble” (Malachi 2:7-8).
passages.hard:
Does verse 51 mean that the Jewish people carry the guilt of these murders, then or now? No. Jesus is speaking to leaders of his own day about what they themselves are about to do. Scripture forbids putting the guilt of fathers on children: “each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16). For centuries many Christians called the Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’ and used scenes like this to justify contempt, expulsions, and violence against Jews. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: in Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).

‘This generation’ means the people alive in Jesus' day. Many readers link the judgment he warns of to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.
passages.asks: It is easy to honour the prophets of the past and say we would have listened. Ask who is telling you the truth today that you do not want to hear. And if you teach others in any way, as a parent, a leader, a friend, ask whether you are opening the door to God for them, or standing in it.
